title: Risks
summary: What could go wrong, how likely and how bad (1 = low, 5 = high), what we do about it, and which phase checks it.

items.title: Tauri cannot yet give each site its own profile
items.summary: Sites are to be kept apart by separate WebView2 profiles, but a profile can only be set when a web view is created, and Tauri does not pass it through yet.
items.mitigation: Tested in P1: creating the tab views ourselves gives each site its own profile in one shared browser (experiment 2). You choose the route; then the risk can close.

items.title: Multi-view feature may be unstable
items.summary: Many web views in one window needs a Tauri feature marked experimental. Known bugs: hangs, blank views, lost keyboard focus.
items.mitigation: Tested in P1: create views only from background code and keep the shell above the tabs. Copy and paste work; after Alt+Tab the keyboard needs a click (known issue, fix planned in P2).

items.title: Tab sleep and memory saving need unsafe low-level code
items.summary: The WebView2 calls that put a tab to sleep or ask it to use less memory are not in Tauri, so we must reach them through unsafe code. Sleep can also simply fail.
items.mitigation: Tested in P1: every needed engine call works through Tauri. All low-level code stays in one module with written safety rules.

items.title: AMD energy readings may be estimates
items.summary: Research suggests AMD's energy counters are modelled rather than measured, cover only the CPU chip, and need admin rights plus a kernel driver.
items.mitigation: Label every reading as a CPU-chip estimate; system energy only with a wall meter; never the unsafe WinRing0 driver; any driver only with your approval.

items.title: Counting each browser's memory fairly is hard
items.summary: Browsers run many helper processes, some shared. Counting the wrong ones, or double-counting shared memory, would make the main comparison wrong.
items.mitigation: Tested in P1: every web view helper process lands in a Windows job around the app, plus a crash reporter counted separately. Chrome and Edge are checked in P6.

items.title: The test robot sees WebView2 less clearly
items.summary: Playwright reaches WebView2 only through a debugging channel it calls lower fidelity, and an open channel may itself change behaviour.
items.mitigation: Tested in P1: the same robot drives Ferrum, Chrome and Edge, and each tab is visible to it; it measures only the shown tab. The debug-channel overhead is checked in P6.

items.title: Navigation filter could let blocked pages through
items.summary: Tauri's navigation check allows any address it cannot read, and never sees pages loaded inside frames, so a blocked site could slip in.
items.mitigation: Ferrum's own filter refuses unreadable addresses, watches frames through low-level hooks, always handles pop-ups and downloads, and is tested with bad addresses.

items.title: Network log needs low-level code
items.summary: Tauri has no hook that sees normal web traffic, so the network log must use unsafe WebView2 calls, or the debugging channel as a fallback.
items.mitigation: Build it on WebView2's response event; keep the metadata-only format with tests; never log content; keep logs out of git; measure its cost first.

items.title: All web views must share identical start-up settings
items.summary: Web views sharing one data folder must use exactly the same settings (flags, proxy, language) or creation fails, so no per-tab differences.
items.mitigation: Build one settings set at start-up and reuse it everywhere; apply benchmark flags to the whole app; test that a mismatch is rejected early.

items.title: Google sign-in will refuse Ferrum tabs
items.summary: Google's rules block sign-in from embedded web views like Ferrum's tabs, so Google login is expected to fail.
items.mitigation: Never disguise Ferrum to get around it; offer 'open in your normal browser'; document it; pick benchmark sites that need no Google login.

items.title: Browsers update themselves mid-study
items.summary: Chrome, Edge and WebView2 update automatically. A version change during a measurement run makes the results incomparable.
items.mitigation: Record exact versions in every trial; stop a run if one changes; run in short windows with updates paused; keep the exact installers used.

items.title: Windows background work and heat add noise
items.summary: Updates, antivirus, indexing, CPU temperature and even window visibility change the numbers, adding noise or bias.
items.mitigation: A recorded checklist before each run; fixed window state; cool-down between trials; products in random order; same-vs-same tests to measure the noise.

items.title: Rivals' power-saving features can skew comparisons
items.summary: Edge and Chrome ship sleeping tabs, Startup Boost and Memory Saver. On or off changes who wins, and switching them off just to help Ferrum is not allowed.
items.mitigation: If you agree, measure as-shipped and a matched setup; set and record every such setting per trial; justify and report anything switched off.

items.title: Our own tools could bias the results
items.summary: The team building Ferrum also builds the benchmark, so bias can creep in through tooling or through choices made after seeing data.
items.mitigation: Fix the main measures and analysis before collecting data; validate tools with same-vs-same tests; instrument every browser alike; analyse every run.

items.title: A session can stop mid-change and lose state
items.summary: Sessions run out of tokens. A stop in the middle of a multi-file change can leave broken work or a wrong status page.
items.mitigation: After every task: update the status page and log, commit locally. Keep tasks small, write handoff notes early, check status against git on restart.

items.title: Scope creep: two equal goals, no tie-breaker
items.summary: The app and the research weigh the same and both wish lists are long, so work can grow without anyone deciding it should.
items.mitigation: Freeze each phase's work list when you approve it; new ideas go to a backlog or a decision you approve; compare effort to the estimate at each review.

items.title: Our tab-sleep policy may not be new
items.summary: Chrome, Edge, ChromeOS and Android already freeze, sleep or discard tabs. Claiming novelty without a proper literature review would be wrong.
items.mitigation: A systematic literature review in P8 before any novelty claim; claim only what it supports; report null results honestly.

items.title: Bugs in unsafe low-level code
items.summary: Several features need unsafe Windows code. Mistakes there can crash Ferrum, leak memory, or keep closed tabs alive.
items.mitigation: One module behind a safe interface; every unsafe block documented; handlers that remove themselves; leak and crash tests; checklist review of each change.

items.title: A change could expose Ferrum's internals to websites
items.summary: Every web view can technically message Ferrum's Rust code. A configuration slip could let a website run privileged commands or weaken isolation.
items.mitigation: Commands only for the trusted controls, never for websites; tabs blocked from Ferrum's own pages; security tests from P2, fully in P4, and on every upgrade.

items.title: Tools and libraries change under us
items.summary: Over months, Tauri, Node, TypeScript, ESLint and Mermaid release new major versions that can break the build.
items.mitigation: Pin exact versions and commit lock files; record installed versions in P1; upgrade only as a planned task that re-runs all tests; audit dependencies.

items.title: One machine may not speak for all
items.summary: All results come from one AMD desktop. Memory and process behaviour depend on the machine, so results may not hold elsewhere.
items.mitigation: State the one-machine scope in every result; record full hardware details; publish tools and raw data; add a second machine only if you have one.

items.title: Approval records could be wrong
items.summary: Phases start only when approvals match the current pages. A fingerprint bug, a corrupt file, or an approval you never gave would start or block work wrongly.
items.mitigation: Claude records approvals only after saving your words, via one tested script that stores page fingerprints; all logged in git. Checked 11 Oct: a fresh copy keeps wiki line endings, so fingerprints hold.

items.title: Sleeping or closing a tab could lose your work
items.summary: If Ferrum sleeps or discards a tab during a download, a call, or while you are typing, data could be lost.
items.mitigation: Exempt tabs with media, downloads, camera or mic, unsaved input, or your exclusions; prefer sleep over discard; adaptive policy off by default; safety tests in P7.

items.title: Your reviews can become a bottleneck
items.summary: Every phase waits for your approval, and any edit to an approved page needs re-approval. Reviews piling up can stall work.
items.mitigation: One review packet per gate showing what changed; batch edits so pages go stale once per round; keep doing independent work; ask questions early.

items.title: Too few trials to see real differences
items.summary: With about 30 trials per setup only fairly large differences are detectable; small but meaningful ones could be missed.
items.mitigation: Size runs from the measured noise; fix main measures and thresholds in advance; correct for many comparisons; report confidence ranges and effect sizes.
